title: Paper to Portfolio: a local Gemma reads the old share certificate in your drawer, but never does the maths
summary:
This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 3: Slow and Steady

What I Built

Lots of Indian families have a drawer with a few old share certificates in it: thick, cream-coloured paper, a company seal, "100 Equity Shares of Rs. 10/- each", dated sometime in the 1980s. Nobody knows what they are worth. The company on the paper usually no longer exists under that name. Since then there have been bonus issues, a stock split, maybe a merger. And if the dividends went unclaimed for seven years in a row, the shares may have been moved to the government's Investor Education and Protection Fund (IEPF).

Working that out today means weeks of digging through exchange filings, or paying a share-recovery firm.

Paper to Portfolio does it on your own laptop in about five minutes:

  1. Photograph the certificate. A local Gemma model reads the company, holder, folio, certificate number, share count, face value and date.
  2. Paste the company's corporate-announcement history, copied from the exchange website or annual reports.
  3. Gemma picks out every bonus, split, merger and rename, and must quote the sentence it relied on.
  4. Plain Python checks every quote against your text and does all the arithmetic, with exact fractions.
  5. You get the lineage timeline, the share count and value today, a plain-language explanation (English, Hindi, Marathi, Bengali or Tamil), and a claim checklist: IEPF search, RTA, KYC, transmission, demat, IEPF-5.

Shares held for 35 years without anyone touching them are the most slow-and-steady investment there is. This tool lets the tortoise collect its winnings.

Demo

The screenshots come from a real run on my laptop, and the voice-over is generated with ElevenLabs (eleven_multilingual_v2).

The demo uses a fictional specimen certificate and a made-up company, both in the repo, so anyone can reproduce it:

1989: 100 shares of Sahyadri Spinning Mills, face value Rs 10
→ 1994 bonus 1:1 → 200
→ 2001 bonus 1:2 → 300
→ 2006 split Rs 10 to Rs 2 → 1,500
→ 2011 merged into Deccan Textiles, 3 for every 4 → 1,125
→ 2018 renamed Deccan Fabtech
Today: 1,125 shares, 11.25x, worth Rs 4,64,062.50 at a Rs 412.50 share price

On my CPU-only laptop, reading the certificate takes 38 to 84 seconds (depending on whether the model is already loaded), and tracing plus the summary takes about 3 minutes 15 seconds. No GPU, no hurry.

Rahullkumr / paper-to-portfolio

Hacktoberfest Week 3 DEV Challenge - Slow and Steady

Paper to Portfolio

Found an old share certificate in a drawer? Paper to Portfolio reads it with a local open-weight model, traces every bonus, split, merger and rename since the day it was printed, and tells you what it is worth today and how to claim it.

Thousands of Indian families hold physical shares bought in the 1980s and 90s. The company has usually been renamed or merged, the share count has multiplied several times, and unclaimed dividends may have been moved to the IEPF. Working that out by hand takes weeks, or a paid recovery firm. Here it takes a few slow minutes on a laptop with no GPU.

How it works

  1. Read. Gemma (gemma4:e4b, via Ollama) reads the certificate photo into structured fields: company, holder, folio, certificate number, shares, face value, issue date. You check and correct them.
  2. Extract. You paste the company's corporate-announcement history (from…
View on GitHub

How I Built It

Stack: Python 3.12 standard library only, plus Ollama running gemma4:e4b locally. One small web page, no framework, no cloud.

The whole design comes down to one rule: let the model read and write, never let it count.

Reading: Gemma vision with a JSON schema. The certificate photo goes to Gemma through Ollama's chat API with a strict JSON schema (company, holder, folio, certificate_no, shares, face_value, issue_date). On my test certificate it got every field right on the first try. The page still shows the fields as editable boxes, because a 40-year-old photocopy will be harder.

Extracting: evidence or it didn't happen. Exchange filings are full of noise: dividends, AGMs, board meetings. Gemma gets the pasted history and returns only share-changing events. Each event has typed fields (give/per for bonus and merger ratios, from_fv/to_fv for splits, into for the new company name) and an evidence string that must be copied word for word.

Verifying: the model's output is a proposal, not a fact. ledger.verify() normalises whitespace and case, then checks that each evidence string really appears in the source text. It also rejects events with missing ratios or unreadable dates. An invented "5:1 bonus" gets thrown out and shown in red on the page. Two things caught me on the first run: Gemma echoed Indian DD-MM-YYYY dates back, and left out the ratio fields when the schema didn't require them. The fix was to make every field required (0 when it doesn't apply) and parse both date styles in code.

Computing: fractions.Fraction, not floats, not the LLM. Bonus 1:2 multiplies by 3/2. A split from Rs 10 to Rs 2 multiplies by 5. A 3-for-4 merger multiplies by 3/4. After each step the count is floored, because Indian companies pool fractional entitlements, sell them and pay cash. The fraction is kept and shown.

Explaining: Gemma gets the computed facts only. The summary prompt passes in the finished timeline and says use only these numbers. The claim checklist is fixed text written by a person, because a wrong legal step can cost a family months.

Tests cover the sample lineage end to end, fraction flooring, consolidation, events before the issue date, invented evidence, missing ratios and the transmission step. They need no model, so GitHub Actions runs them on every push.

Why Does Open Innovation Matter?

A share certificate carries a family's full name, folio number and holdings, often of someone who has died. That's exactly the kind of document people shouldn't have to upload to somebody else's server to understand. With an open-weight model running on the laptop, the certificate never leaves the house. That matters more than raw accuracy: a closed API would be quicker, but it asks families to trust a third party with the paper that proves what they own.

Open weights also made the trust design possible. Because I control the model, the prompt and the schema, I could build the tool around not trusting it: structured output, quoted evidence, code-side checks, code-side arithmetic. The model is a fast reader that works for the code. And because the whole thing is MIT-licensed and runs on a CPU, an investor-awareness group or a small-town CA can run it for people who would never pay a recovery firm.

My Agent Session

I planned and built this with Claude Code, and the full session is captured with Entire, unedited, because it explains why this code exists. The first half is idea research: I went through more than 25 ideas, and the agent searched DEV and GitHub and found almost every one already built this month (forward checkers, chat digests, file tidiers, read-later bots, trading journals). This idea was the first with no existing AI tool, only paid recovery firms. The second half is the build, including the date-format bug.

Session and checkpoints: https://entire.com/gh/Rahullkumr/paper-to-portfolio/commit/83893ddd41a6b0a02eb171d1582772a11948174d

The Lazy Payoff

By hand Paper to Portfolio
Read the certificate squint, type under 90 s
Find every bonus, split, merger, rename days in exchange archives paste once, about 3 min
Do the maths across 35 years spreadsheet plus doubt exact, with sources
Know what to do next ask around checklist

Total for the sample: under 5 minutes of laptop time and about 30 seconds of mine.

Prize Categories

  • Best Use of Gemma: gemma4:e4b locally for vision OCR, evidence-quoted extraction and multilingual explanation.
  • Best Use of Entire: the unedited agent session behind the project is linked above, including the research that shows why this idea was chosen.
  • Best Use of GitHub Copilot: GitHub Actions runs the test suite on every push.
  • Best Use of ElevenLabs: the demo narration is generated with ElevenLabs.

The sample certificate, company and holder are fictional. This is general guidance, not legal or financial advice; confirm with the company's RTA or the IEPF Authority before filing anything. Written with AI assistance and edited by me.

title: PatchGarden 🌱: I Built an AI Maintenance Engineer That Doesn't Trust Its Own Patches
summary:
This is my submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge: Week 3 — Slow and Steady.

PatchGarden 🌱: I Built an AI Maintenance Engineer That Doesn't Trust Its Own Patches

AI can write code in seconds. But when it breaks your repository, who makes sure the fix actually works?

We've reached a point where generating code is becoming easier than ever. AI coding tools can suggest implementations, explain errors, and produce patches almost instantly.

But there's a problem I kept coming back to:

Generating a fix is easy. Knowing whether it's safe to trust that fix is a different problem.

A patch can look convincing, modify the right-looking file, and still introduce a regression. A green-looking AI response doesn't mean the bug is gone.

Meanwhile, open-source maintainers are left dealing with failing tests, neglected issues, dependency problems, and maintenance work that never seems to end.

For Hacktoberfest's Slow and Steady challenge, I wanted to explore a different approach.

Instead of building another AI tool that generates more code, I wanted to build something that helps developers spend less time babysitting maintenance work.

Meet PatchGarden — an AI-powered repository maintenance project built around one principle:

Don't trust a patch because AI generated it. Collect evidence, verify the result, and let the developer decide.

🌿 What is PatchGarden?

PatchGarden is designed to help developers investigate repository failures, generate minimal repair proposals, verify changes, and preserve an auditable history of the process.

Think of a developer who returns to a project after months away. There are failing tests, an issue backlog, and a bug report that nobody has had time to investigate.

Instead of manually navigating every step, the developer can delegate a focused maintenance task to PatchGarden.

The intended workflow is:

Investigate → Plan → Patch → Verify → Review

Here's what each stage means:

  • Investigate: Inspect relevant code and diagnostic evidence to understand the reported failure.
  • Plan: Produce a structured repair plan with a clear hypothesis and defined verification criteria.
  • Patch: Generate a minimal, reviewable candidate change in an isolated workspace.
  • Verify: Run the relevant tests and compare the results against the baseline.
  • Review: Present the diff and evidence so a human can approve or reject the proposed repair.

If the evidence is insufficient or the tests fail, the system should report that honestly instead of pretending the task succeeded.

The goal isn't autonomous code modification at any cost. It's making repository maintenance less tedious without sacrificing developer control.

🦥 Why does this fit Slow and Steady?

Software maintenance is rarely one dramatic task. It's hundreds of small jobs that developers keep postponing.

Investigate that failing test. Reproduce that bug. Check that dependency. Review that patch. Rerun the suite. Figure out what happened when the process failed halfway through.

Individually, these tasks seem manageable. Collectively, they become maintenance debt.

PatchGarden explores how open-source AI can help with that repetitive work while keeping the developer responsible for the final decision.

The Lazy Payoff

Delegate the investigation. Review the evidence. Spend your attention where it actually matters.

Rather than trying to replace the developer, PatchGarden aims to remove the repetitive work surrounding a repair.

🧠 The important engineering decision: AI proposes, tools verify

I didn't want the entire application to depend on a model saying, "I've fixed it."

An AI model can produce malformed output, misunderstand a code path, or confidently suggest an incorrect repair. That means the model cannot be the authority on whether a patch is correct.

The architecture separates reasoning from execution:

1. Open-weight AI for investigation

The project is designed around Google's open-weight Gemma 3 (4B) running locally on Ollama. A smaller local model creates a healthy engineering constraint: instead of assuming a massive cloud model can magically fix everything, the system limits the context, validates structured JSON outputs, and relies on deterministic tooling for execution. Local inference keeps repository code private and eliminates external API token fees.

2. A controlled execution layer

Repository inspection, Git operations, test execution, and workflow state are handled by explicit application logic rather than arbitrary model-generated shell commands. Model output is treated as untrusted input. Paths are validated, operations are restricted to isolated Git worktrees, and candidate changes are kept strictly quarantined from the main branch.

3. Independent verification

The system distinguishes between generating a patch and demonstrating that the patch passes configured checks. A complete repair record contains:

  • The original failure and diagnostic evidence.
  • The proposed change and Git diff.
  • The verification commands and their exit codes.
  • Any errors or regressions encountered.
  • The final maintainer review decision.

Passing tests don't prove that every bug is fixed. They provide evidence that the candidate passes the checks we actually ran. That distinction matters.

♻️ What happens when the process stops halfway through?

A maintenance workflow can take multiple steps. A process can crash, a model can time out, or a machine can restart before the job finishes. Simply storing the active task in application memory is not enough.

PatchGarden relies on Temporal durable workflow orchestration paired with persistent SQLite domain state (patchgarden.db) and immutable JSONL audit logs. Workflow state transitions are recorded before and after each phase. If the worker process restarts mid-repair, Temporal rehydrates the execution history, validates saved checkpoints, and resumes execution without re-running completed work or dirtying the repository.

🔓 Why open innovation matters

Open-source AI is not just a label in PatchGarden's technology stack. It creates an opportunity to design the system around model choice, inspectable behavior, and developer-controlled infrastructure:

  • Model flexibility: Maintainers can swap models or run different quantization levels locally.
  • Local inference & privacy: Source code, proprietary internal libraries, and sensitive test logs never leave the developer's workstation.
  • Cost control: Local open-weight models have zero token fees, allowing extensive multi-stage investigation and repair loops.
  • Transparency: The entire toolchain—from prompt schemas to worktree managers—is open-source and inspectable.

🛠️ How I built it

PatchGarden brings together a broadsheet-inspired web interface, a typed backend API, a durable worker engine, and local open-weight AI:

  • Project repository: GitHub — Neet2516/PatchGarden
  • Live application: https://patchgarden-web.onrender.com
  • Technologies:
    • Frontend: Next.js 14 (App Router, React, CSS)
    • API: Fastify (Node.js & TypeScript)
    • Durable Orchestration: Temporal Cloud / Temporal local server
    • Persistence: SQLite (better-sqlite3) & structured JSONL audit logs
    • Inference Runtime: Gemma 3 (4B) via local Ollama
    • Isolation: Git worktrees for clean verification environments
    • Deployment: Render (Hosting the web dashboard and API)

📸 Application Interface & Candidate Patch Review

Here is the live interface running in production on Render:

🎥 See PatchGarden in action

  • Watch the demo: PatchGarden — YouTube
  • Try the application: https://patchgarden-web.onrender.com
  • Explore the source code: https://github.com/Neet2516/PatchGarden

The most important part of a demonstration is not how confidently the AI explains its answer. It's whether the workflow produces inspectable evidence of what happened.

🧪 What I would measure next

A trustworthy maintenance tool needs more than a polished interface. I would evaluate PatchGarden against a reproducible benchmark of deliberately seeded bugs and measure:

  1. Root-cause identification accuracy.
  2. Clean patch application rates across diverse codebases.
  3. Test suite pass rates and regression detection sensitivity.
  4. Workflow recovery fidelity across simulated power and worker outages.
  5. In-flight token latency and memory footprint of local 4B models.
  6. The accuracy of the system's "refusal to patch" when diagnostic evidence is ambiguous.

🌱 What comes next?

The long-term direction is a maintenance assistant that developers can trust with repetitive investigations without surrendering control of their repositories. That means deeper AST-aware repair suggestions, tighter containerized sandboxing, reproducible evaluations, and clearer explanations of uncertainty.

The goal isn't to build an AI that never makes mistakes. It's to build a system that makes mistakes visible, limits their impact, and refuses to confuse a plausible answer with a verified result.

🏆 Prize Categories

  • Best Use of Render:

PatchGarden's production web dashboard and API service are deployed on Render at https://patchgarden-web.onrender.com using a multi-service render.yaml blueprint with monorepo build orchestration.

  • Best Use of Temporal:

PatchGarden uses Temporal for durable workflow orchestration, enabling maintenance jobs to progress through defined stages with workflow state, retries, and recovery. This integration supports the project's central goal: making repository maintenance reliable even when individual steps fail.

  • Local AI with Ollama :

PatchGarden uses Ollama as its local model inference runtime, allowing the application to run a supported model locally for repository analysis and repair proposals. This supports experimentation with open-weight AI while keeping model execution separate from deterministic patch verification.

🤖 My Agent Session

Here is the genuine DevRelay agent session documenting the end-to-end development, debugging, and deployment of PatchGarden:

💬 I'd love your feedback

If you maintain open-source projects, what's the maintenance task you keep putting off? Is it reproducing bugs, triaging issues, fixing flaky tests, or reviewing changes generated by AI?

I'd love to learn which part of this workflow would save maintainers the most time—and what evidence you'd need before trusting an AI-proposed patch.

Slow and steady. Evidence before assumptions. Verification before approval.

Instead of building another AI tool that generates more code, I wanted to build something that helps developers spend less time babysitting maintenance work.

Meet PatchGarden — an AI-powered repository maintenance project built around one principle:

Don't trust a patch because AI generated it. Collect evidence, verify the result, and let the developer decide.

🌿 What is PatchGarden?

PatchGarden is designed to help developers investigate repository failures, generate minimal repair proposals, verify changes, and preserve an auditable history of the process.

Think of a developer who returns to a project after months away. There are failing tests, an issue backlog, and a bug report that nobody has had time to investigate.

Instead of manually navigating every step, the developer can delegate a focused maintenance task to PatchGarden.

The intended workflow is:

Investigate → Plan → Patch → Verify → Review

Here's what each stage means:

  • Investigate: Inspect relevant code and diagnostic evidence to understand the reported failure.
  • Plan: Produce a structured repair plan with a clear hypothesis and defined verification criteria.
  • Patch: Generate a minimal, reviewable candidate change in an isolated workspace.
  • Verify: Run the relevant tests and compare the results against the baseline.
  • Review: Present the diff and evidence so a human can approve or reject the proposed repair.

If the evidence is insufficient or the tests fail, the system should report that honestly instead of pretending the task succeeded.

The goal isn't autonomous code modification at any cost. It's making repository maintenance less tedious without sacrificing developer control.

🦥 Why does this fit Slow and Steady?

Software maintenance is rarely one dramatic task. It's hundreds of small jobs that developers keep postponing.

Investigate that failing test. Reproduce that bug. Check that dependency. Review that patch. Rerun the suite. Figure out what happened when the process failed halfway through.

Individually, these tasks seem manageable. Collectively, they become maintenance debt.

PatchGarden explores how open-source AI can help with that repetitive work while keeping the developer responsible for the final decision.

The Lazy Payoff

Delegate the investigation. Review the evidence. Spend your attention where it actually matters.

Rather than trying to replace the developer, PatchGarden aims to remove the repetitive work surrounding a repair.

🧠 The important engineering decision: AI proposes, tools verify

I didn't want the entire application to depend on a model saying, "I've fixed it."

An AI model can produce malformed output, misunderstand a code path, or confidently suggest an incorrect repair. That means the model cannot be the authority on whether a patch is correct.

The architecture separates reasoning from execution:

1. Open-weight AI for investigation

The project is designed around Google's open-weight Gemma 3 (4B) running locally on Ollama. A smaller local model creates a healthy engineering constraint: instead of assuming a massive cloud model can magically fix everything, the system limits the context, validates structured JSON outputs, and relies on deterministic tooling for execution. Local inference keeps repository code private and eliminates external API token fees.

2. A controlled execution layer

Repository inspection, Git operations, test execution, and workflow state are handled by explicit application logic rather than arbitrary model-generated shell commands. Model output is treated as untrusted input. Paths are validated, operations are restricted to isolated Git worktrees, and candidate changes are kept strictly quarantined from the main branch.

3. Independent verification

The system distinguishes between generating a patch and demonstrating that the patch passes configured checks. A complete repair record contains:

  • The original failure and diagnostic evidence.
  • The proposed change and Git diff.
  • The verification commands and their exit codes.
  • Any errors or regressions encountered.
  • The final maintainer review decision.

A maintenance workflow can take multiple steps. A process can crash, a model can time out, or a machine can restart before the job finishes. Simply storing the active task in application memory is not enough.

🔓 Why open innovation matters

Open-source AI is not just a label in PatchGarden's technology stack. It creates an opportunity to design the system around model choice, inspectable behavior, and developer-controlled infrastructure:

  • Model flexibility: Maintainers can swap models or run different quantization levels locally.
  • Local inference & privacy: Source code, proprietary internal libraries, and sensitive test logs never leave the developer's workstation.
  • Cost control: Local open-weight models have zero token fees, allowing extensive multi-stage investigation and repair loops.
  • Transparency: The entire toolchain—from prompt schemas to worktree managers—is open-source and inspectable.

🛠️ How I built it

PatchGarden brings together a broadsheet-inspired web interface, a typed backend API, a durable worker engine, and local open-weight AI:

  • Live application: https://patchgarden-web.onrender.com

    • Frontend: Next.js 14 (App Router, React, CSS)
    • API: Fastify (Node.js & TypeScript)
    • Durable Orchestration: Temporal Cloud / Temporal local server
    • Persistence: SQLite (better-sqlite3) & structured JSONL audit logs
    • Inference Runtime: Gemma 3 (4B) via local Ollama
    • Isolation: Git worktrees for clean verification environments
    • Deployment: Render (Hosting the web dashboard and API)

A trustworthy maintenance tool needs more than a polished interface. I would evaluate PatchGarden against a reproducible benchmark of deliberately seeded bugs and measure:

  1. Root-cause identification accuracy.
  2. Clean patch application rates across diverse codebases.
  3. Test suite pass rates and regression detection sensitivity.
  4. Workflow recovery fidelity across simulated power and worker outages.
  5. In-flight token latency and memory footprint of local 4B models.
  6. The accuracy of the system's "refusal to patch" when diagnostic evidence is ambiguous.

🌱 What comes next?

The long-term direction is a maintenance assistant that developers can trust with repetitive investigations without surrendering control of their repositories. That means deeper AST-aware repair suggestions, tighter containerized sandboxing, reproducible evaluations, and clearer explanations of uncertainty.

The goal isn't to build an AI that never makes mistakes. It's to build a system that makes mistakes visible, limits their impact, and refuses to confuse a plausible answer with a verified result.

title: DocDrift: Your Code Drifted. Your Docs Didn't Have To.
summary:
This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 3: Slow and Steady

What I Built

DocDrift — a background watcher that keeps your docs honest, powered entirely by open-source AI.

The Problem-----

Here's the loop it breaks. You ship a feature. An env var gets renamed, a default port changes, an endpoint moves to /v2. Your README is now quietly fiction, and somewhere between "I'll update it in the next commit" and "the next commit turned into 40," the docs die. Empirical research backs the feeling — the ICSME 2023 study on outdated documentation references ("Detecting Outdated Code Element References in Software Documentation") found docs routinely pointing at code elements deleted many revisions ago. And notably, string-matching tools can only flag references whose occurrences drop to zero — a changed default like PORT 3000 → 8080 sails straight past them, because the string still exists. DocDrift compares values and shapes, not just string existence.

What it actually does:

  • Parses the real AST, not vibes. tree-sitter WASM grammars extract exported functions, classes, interfaces, routes and config keys from your TypeScript and Python files, each with line-precise evidence. If a grammar chokes on exotic syntax, a structural fallback extractor takes over and the miss lands in a queryable failure ledger. On the docs side, your README tables, setup guides and .env.example are parsed into typed targets with the same rigor — so both sides of the comparison speak the same language.
  • Runs a nine-step agent crew with two validation gates. A Mastra workflow (doc-drift-sync) chains intake → extract → docs → synthesize → gate-1 → patch → gate-2 → tone → emit into one typed, inspectable graph. Gemma drafts the findings; Gate 1 then drops every claim the AST can't prove — no phantom links survive — and Gate 2 applies the proposed patch to a shadow copy of your docs, re-parses it, and refuses edits that would break a markdown table.
  • Gives you a reviewable PR, not a robot merge. The output is a unified diff, a humanized PR title and body, and a full step trace with timings. You review. That is the whole job. PRs open from a docdrift/docs-sync- branch against your default branch — never auto-merged.

There are two ways to use it. The Studio: sign in with GitHub (your own account, your own token — DocDrift never holds an org-wide key), pick a repo, branch and doc file, and watch the whole pipeline run live. Or the autopilot: install a push webhook on your repo, and every push that drifts the docs opens a docs-sync PR without you opening anything. HMAC-SHA256 verified, scoped to the installer's session, one user can't trigger another's webhook.

The three sloth-things baked in: it waits for your push (webhook events, not cron polling), it does the boring comparison work, and it stops before the risky part — merging is your call.

Demo

Try it in about 30 seconds at https://docdrift-rfjj.onrender.com

Code

Repo: https://github.com/N-Garai/DocDrift

DocDrift was built by pair-programming with a rotating cast of AI coding agents — DeepSeek, Kilo Code, GitHub Copilot and opencode — each picked for what it was good at: DeepSeek for heavy reasoning and big-picture design, Kilo Code and opencode for rulebook-driven implementation sprints, and Copilot for inline completions and roadmap development. But the code generation was never the interesting part — the discipline was.

How I Built It

The constraint I set from day one: the open pieces have to be what makes the project work — not a coat of paint over a proprietary core. Everything below is verifiable in the repo, file by file.

  • Mastra as the agent harness. Four specialized Mastra Agent instances share one job: extraction, validation (Gate 1), patching (Gate 2) and tone. They're wired into a real Mastra workflow via createWorkflow/createStep — nine typed steps chained with .then() and committed as one graph. Every step's input and output is a Zod schema, so an LLM can't sneak a malformed finding past the type system, and every run produces a replayable step trace.
  • tree-sitter as the compiler for prose. web-tree-sitter with prebuilt grammars from @repomix/tree-sitter-wasms gives line-precise symbol extraction for TypeScript and Python. Parser failures are recorded in an in-memory ledger (last 50, surfaced at GET /api/health) and shipped to Sentry with a redacting beforeSend — cookies, tokens and session IDs never leave the machine.
  • Gemma as the prose engine, in a provider chain. The reasoning layer resolves per request, with a 15-second cached verdict: local Ollama Gemma (default gemma3:4b at localhost:11434) → the free Gemini API tier serving the open-weight gemma-4-31b-it → and finally a deterministic comparator engine — a rule-based drift detector (changed defaults, missing symbols, rename detection via similarity scoring ≥ 0.62, orphaned doc targets, env keys, stale routes) that produces the same artifact with zero network calls. Temperature 0.2, explicit timeouts and retries — and the chain is one env var to reconfigure.
  • The two gates are the anti-hallucination core. The design leans on the documentation-drift literature, all annotated in docs/RESEARCH.md: Ratol & Robillard's DOCREF ("Detecting API Documentation Errors", OOPSLA 2014) and the 2025 Concordia LLM traceability study ("Evaluating the Use of LLMs for Documentation-to-Code Traceability") both document how "phantom links" pervade LLM-linked docs. So Gate 1 re-checks every Gemma finding against the extracted symbols and drops anything the AST cannot prove before a patch is built. Gate 2 does the mirror check on the docs side: apply the edit to a snapshot, re-parse it, confirm tables stay well-formed and the symbol is genuinely documented now. Broken edits get repaired once, then flagged — never silently merged.

The whole stack is Bun + TypeScript, Express on the engine, Next.js front end, a zero-dependency JSON store for sessions and webhook registrations (no database required — swap in Postgres later behind the same interface), node:test for the test suite, and a multi-stage Dockerfile whose single Node process serves the API and the static-exported frontend on one port. On the building side, I pair-programmed the codebase with agentic coding tools — DeepSeek, Kilo Code, GitHub Copilot and opencode — under a rulebook the whole team (human included) had to follow.

Why Does Open Innovation Matter?

DocDrift reads code, docs and env files from your repository — the payload a closed tool would demand you upload somewhere. Open makes the trust question easy to answer:

  • Your repos stay local. The default inference path is Ollama on localhost; the deterministic engine doesn't even open a socket. Anyone can verify that by reading core/llm/provider.ts — which is exactly the point. Closed-source doc tools ask you to trust the pipeline; open-source lets you audit the pipeline.
  • It costs nothing to run, forever. Every component — Mastra, tree-sitter, Gemma weights, the Ollama runtime — is free, and the free Gemini tier is a fallback, not a crutch. The landing page's live demo runs with zero providers configured (the deterministic engine powers it). There's no paid plan to outgrow, no credit card, no trial clock.
  • The brain is swappable by config, not migration. Set OLLAMA_MODEL, point at another local model, or drop the key and use the deterministic engine. Fine-tuning how your agent behaves is an env edit.
  • Honest intelligence. The similarity thresholds, the evidence rules, the gate behavior — it's all in plain TypeScript with 36 tests over it rather than a marketing page. That transparency is only possible when the core is open.

My Agent Session

The build was pair-programmed with a rotating cast of AI coding agents — DeepSeek Harness, Kilo Code, GitHub Copilot and opencode — different tools for different jobs, and the interesting part was the discipline, not the code generation.

The Lazy Payoff

The honest math: every time you ship anything, keeping your own backlog of docs consistent is a 20–30 minute guilt-tax — reread the README, scan your config keys against .env.example, and see if the endpoints match. Most weeks, the honest answer is that nobody does it, and the tables fall behind. DocDrift does not ask you to remember anything.

  • Studio path: click through the repo picker, hit "Run drift analysis," get the diff. The demo runs on the landing page in a browser with no API key of any kind, so the price of admission to "my docs are freshly audited" is one click.
  • Webhook path: install once, forget. Every push lands a review PR whenever your docs fall out of date with the code. You review and merge whenever you want — DocDrift will never merge for you, which is exactly the design decision you want from a tool handling your README.
  • When it's wrong, it fails loudly: the mandatory evidence rules mean the diff is a real diff with real files, and the failure ledger at /api/health shows you exactly what the parser missed instead of hiding it.

The sloth wins because I only do the part that needs a human: deciding whether the new table row reads well.

Prize Categories

  • Best Use of Gemma — Gemma's open weights are the reasoning engine at the center of the synthesize step, with a provider chain covering both real deployment modes: local via Ollama (default gemma3:4b) on the laptop path and the open-weight gemma-4-31b-it on the hosted free tier (temperature 0.2, explicit timeouts, structured Zod outputs), plus a deterministic fallback so the pipeline never stalls without a provider.
  • Best Use of Mastra — the entire brain runs on the open Mastra harness: four specialized Agent instances wired into one production createWorkflow graph (doc-drift-sync) of nine typed createSteps (intake → extract → docs → synthesize → gate-1 → patch → gate-2 → tone → emit), all with Zod-typed step boundaries and per-step traces replayable in the Studio.
  • Best Use of Render — DocDrift is deployed on Render's free tier (render.yaml, Docker service): health check on /api/health, auto-deploy, production env wiring for the GitHub OAuth app and webhook secret — and a custom keep-warm service that self-pings only in production (every 13.5 minutes, cancellable with KEEP_WARM=off) so the free instance doesn't nap through its own ~15-minute idle window.
  • Best Use of Sentry Agent Tracing — the engine instruments its failure paths with @sentry/node (captureParserFailure, captureWorkflowError in core/sentry.ts): every tree-sitter grammar failure and workflow error is captured with a redacting beforeSend that scrubs cookies, GitHub tokens and session IDs before anything leaves, and the same failures surface live in GET /api/health's parser-failure ledger — the observability story includes what you can see without an account.

title: SlothBox: a local file butler that files your downloads, screenshots and receipts while you do nothing
summary:
This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge: Week 3, Slow and Steady.

What I Built

SlothBox watches the folders you choose on a Windows PC, such as Downloads and Screenshots. When a new file lands, a local Gemma model reads it and says what it is: a receipt, a screenshot, a document, or something else. SlothBox then gives the file a clear name, moves it into a sorted folder, and, if it is a receipt, writes a row in a monthly ledger. A page you open on your phone over home Wi-Fi sends photos into the same pipeline. Every move can be undone from the dashboard or the tray.

Nothing leaves the PC. Gemma runs in Docker on your own GPU, the database is a local Postgres, and there is no account.

Who gets lazier

Anyone with a Downloads folder they have stopped looking at, a screenshot pile named Screenshot 2026-10-14 213055.png, or a wallet of paper receipts they mean to type into a spreadsheet one day.

Gemma never writes a file name. It returns fields, and plain code builds the name from a template:

title: I built an open-source tool to edit Jetpack Compose on-device via AST mutations (No Gradle rebuilds)
summary:
Every Android developer knows the frustration of the iteration loop in Jetpack Compose. While Live Edit has improved, it remains volatile—your changes disappear the moment the process restarts. On the other hand, triggering a full Gradle build just to tweak padding, colors, or layout hierarchy eats up minutes of valuable engineering time.

To solve this, I built ComposeBridge—an open-source system that decouples UI tuning from your physical workstation and turns your actual device into a live AST code controller.

🛠 How It Works Under the Hood

ComposeBridge isn't just an in-memory preview swapper. It applies permanent, compile-ready modifications:

  1. AST-Guided Source Mutation: When you adjust a UI token or modifier on your physical device, the operational delta is sent back to your host machine over an encrypted tunnel. A headless background daemon uses Tree-sitter to parse the Kotlin source tree, locate the exact Composable call site, and safely mutate the source file directly on disk.
  2. Visual Diff & Granular Rollbacks: Every file modified by the remote client is buffered. You can review color-coded visual diffs directly on your phone and tap [Accept All / Rollback] to ensure code integrity.
  3. Remote Over-The-Air (OTA) Builds: When you're ready for a full run, trigger a headless Gradle build remotely. The progress is streamed back to your phone, and the compiled APK is pushed and installed over-the-air.
  4. Model Context Protocol (MCP) Server: Features a built-in MCP server exposing 27 tools, allowing external AI coding agents to inspect the AST, analyze tokens, and perform autonomous refactoring loops.

I am actively looking for Android / Compose engineers to test the integration and provide architectural feedback on:

  • Developer experience across different screen sizes.

title: Notes on the technical choices behind glocker, a Linux blocker I can’t switch off
summary:
I spent some time creating a tool to block sites and apps based on schedules as well as to track behaviour. This is an overview of how it works.

The application is completely open source and available at the official site

Blocking

Blocking is done by putting domains into /etc/hosts, pointed at localhost, and the file is made immutable with chattr +i. A small server on 127.0.0.1 answers those requests with a blocked page and logs the hit. The domains are fetched from public blocklists. Domains which have web based proxies are also blocked. A Firefox/Chrome extension, force-installed through the browsers' enterprise policies, catches keywords in URLs and page content. Programs on a list are killed during their windows. Repeated violations run a command of your choice, usually a screen lock you can't dismiss until it times out.

Taking away sudo

If glocker is uninstalled, all protections are lifted. This is prevented by allowing only root to uninstall it and then removing root access during specified windows. During the hours you choose, your sudo line is the full one; outside them it's a short list of harmless commands. glocker writes that line to its own file, /etc/sudoers.d/glocker, validated with visudo first, and swaps it on schedule.

That only works if it's your only sudo, and every distro hands out sudo differently. Debian, Ubuntu and Fedora use a group (sudo or wheel); Arch's installer and Omarchy write a per-user file in sudoers.d; Ubuntu cloud images add a NOPASSWD file of their own. So install has an explicit plan per distro: it removes you from the admin group or moves your file aside, records exactly what it changed, and uninstall puts it back. On a distro without a plan, the sudo window is simply off. An earlier version edited /etc/sudoers directly and broke on Ubuntu's new sudo-rs, which rejects a file without a trailing newline.

glocker -check lists the routes that still get you root: a root password for su, SSH root login, other users with sudo, auto-login. I keep recovery mode open on purpose, as the break-glass.

Making uninstall slow

Now, during the sudo window, it will be possible to uninstall glocker but that can be made annoying enough to prevent you from doing it unless you really need to. glocker -uninstall asks for a reason and then a typing test: a sentence is revealed one character per second, and you type each character as it appears. A wrong key or falling behind starts it over. If you uninstalled recently, the sentence gets longer. It sounds silly, but a minute of typing "I am removing my own guardrails" is usually enough to change your mind.

Watchdog

A small watchdog, glockdoc, pings the daemon every 30 minutes and logs the result, and it survives an uninstall, so a silent teardown still shows up as a gap. With the hosted dashboard, those heartbeats go to a server, and if none arrive for about an hour it emails your accountability partner. This is available on the hosted plan since it requires an email setup.

What the server can see

Synced records are encrypted on the machine before upload. A random master key encrypts window titles, URLs, keywords, app names and reasons per field with AES-GCM; the key is wrapped under your passphrase (PBKDF2-SHA256, 600,000 iterations) and decrypted in the browser. Record IDs are an HMAC under the same key, so they can't be used to guess contents.

Some metadata stays readable, deliberately: timestamps, idle time, window counts, the type of a violation or lifecycle event, and whether a heartbeat arrived. The partner emails need that, and they contain counts and liveness, never what you visited. PBKDF2 isn't memory-hard, so the passphrase has to be strong; the setup page enforces that. I'm not a cryptographer and this hasn't been independently audited.

So install has an explicit plan per distro: it removes you from the admin group or moves your file aside, records exactly what it changed, and uninstall puts it back. On a distro without a plan, the sudo window is simply off. An earlier version edited /etc/sudoers directly and broke on Ubuntu's new sudo-rs, which rejects a file without a trailing newline.

glocker -check lists the routes that still get you root: a root password for su, SSH root login, other users with sudo, auto-login. I keep recovery mode open on purpose, as the break-glass.

Making uninstall slow

Now, during the sudo window, it will be possible to uninstall glocker but that can be made annoying enough to prevent you from doing it unless you really need to. glocker -uninstall asks for a reason and then a typing test: a sentence is revealed one character per second, and you type each character as it appears. A wrong key or falling behind starts it over. If you uninstalled recently, the sentence gets longer. It sounds silly, but a minute of typing "I am removing my own guardrails" is usually enough to change your mind.

Watchdog

A small watchdog, glockdoc, pings the daemon every 30 minutes and logs the result, and it survives an uninstall, so a silent teardown still shows up as a gap. With the hosted dashboard, those heartbeats go to a server, and if none arrive for about an hour it emails your accountability partner. This is available on the hosted plan since it requires an email setup.

What the server can see

Synced records are encrypted on the machine before upload. A random master key encrypts window titles, URLs, keywords, app names and reasons per field with AES-GCM; the key is wrapped under your passphrase (PBKDF2-SHA256, 600,000 iterations) and decrypted in the browser. Record IDs are an HMAC under the same key, so they can't be used to guess contents.

Some metadata stays readable, deliberately: timestamps, idle time, window counts, the type of a violation or lifecycle event, and whether a heartbeat arrived. The partner emails need that, and they contain counts and liveness, never what you visited. PBKDF2 isn't memory-hard, so the passphrase has to be strong; the setup page enforces that. I'm not a cryptographer and this hasn't been independently audited.

title: ProofPack: Automating the Click-Through After the Feature Is Built
summary:
This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 3: Slow and Steady

What I Built

Finishing a feature often leaves another chore: click through it again, check what happened, take screenshots, and assemble an explanation someone else can follow.

I built ProofPack to handle that follow-up work.

ProofPack is an open-source, local-first application that turns a feature brief into a bounded browser demonstration with executable checks and saved evidence. It helps developers demonstrate observable behavior without manually collecting every screenshot and reconstructing every step.

The user supplies an allowlisted application URL, a description of the behavior, and expected outcomes. For example:

Create an account and a project. Log out, open a fresh browser session, and log back in. Verify that the project is still there.

An AI model creates a structured plan and chooses actions from observations of the page. A separate browser worker performs those actions, executes assertions, and records what happened.

The user receives an assertion ledger, an execution timeline, screenshots, downloadable browser traces, and Markdown or self-contained HTML reports.

The distinction I wanted to preserve is simple: asking a model what should happen is different from collecting evidence of what did happen. In ProofPack, the model proposes the work. Executable checks determine the outcome.

Demo

Watch the ProofPack demonstration on YouTube

The video shows ProofPack running locally with real Groq inference against Wikipedia. The request is to search for Go (programming language) using Wikipedia’s search field, then verify the destination URL and visible article title.

Both assertions passed in the final attempt.

Watch the connection between the request, recorded actions, assertion results, and exported evidence. The standalone HTML report includes its screenshots and opens directly from disk.

The video uses selected recording segments with waiting omitted. The article is also opened separately for review after the AI run. An earlier screenshot timeout remains in the run history; the successful retry does not erase it.

I also built two controlled target applications called LaunchDesk. They support the same account-and-project workflow, but one deliberately loses project visibility after a fresh login.

Recorded live Groq runs show the contrast: the working version passed 4/4 checks, while the broken version passed 3/4, failing the final persistence check. Screenshots preserve the observed missing project.

LaunchDesk is a controlled demonstration of the workflow. The Wikipedia example separately exercises a read-only interaction with a public website.

ProofPack itself runs locally; there is no public hosted dashboard.

Code

Source code: github.com/Rohan-Saxena644/ProofPack

The repository contains the application, separate worker, controlled targets, model adapters, verification scripts, screenshots, and recorded verification results.

To try it, install dependencies with npm ci, install Chromium with npm run browsers, copy .env.example to .env, and run npm run dev:all.

The default fixture mode needs no model key. It uses deterministic decisions with a real browser and is explicitly labeled. Live mode requires provider configuration and credentials.

The original application source is MIT-licensed. Dependencies and model weights have their own licenses.

How I Built It

The demonstrated AI configuration uses OpenAI’s open-weight GPT-OSS 120B model, identified as openai/gpt-oss-120b, through Groq’s hosted inference service. Groq serves the model; inference is not running on my laptop.

The execution path starts in a Next.js and React dashboard. The API validates the request and queues it in SQLite. A separate Node.js worker claims the job and runs Playwright Chromium, keeping long browser sessions outside the web request lifecycle.

The planner produces named goals and explicit assertion specifications. Zod validates that structure, including the requirement that every assertion belongs to exactly one goal.

During execution, the worker observes bounded page text and accessible controls. The model receives control IDs, labels, roles, relevant form state, and previously executed actions. It chooses from a small action vocabulary: fill, click, select, navigate, assert, capture, start a fresh browser context, or complete a goal.

The model cannot submit arbitrary JavaScript, selectors, shell commands, or Playwright code. The executor owns those operations.

Assertions currently check exact visible text or exact URLs. Their expected values, observed results, and evidence references are persisted. Finalization checks the ledger before accepting a pass, and report generation checks it again. Reports are assembled deterministically, so a summarizing model cannot rewrite a failed result into a success.

One implementation problem came from the meaning of past actions. Control IDs belong to individual page observations. Earlier live runs repeated work when the model interpreted old IDs against the current page. I added execution provenance, before-and-after URLs, current-goal context, and guards against unchanged repeated actions.

The Wikipedia run exposed another practical limit: long observations could exceed the provider’s token allowance, and full-page screenshots could time out. I compacted model-facing control metadata, bounded the text sent for decisions, and switched evidence capture to viewport screenshots. Text assertions scroll their target into view before capture.

Failure handling also matters. A contradicted assertion is Failed. An unavailable target, exhausted budget, or model problem is Blocked. Worker leases expose interrupted attempts; a manual retry starts fresh browser state and retains earlier evidence.

Shared quota scheduling coordinates workers using the same database, but cannot create additional provider capacity. Exact-origin restrictions constrain browser traffic. Generated passwords are substituted by the executor, masked in screenshots, and redacted from finalized traces.

Verification includes 28 automated unit and improvement tests, eight fixture browser verification groups, and seven additional production UI groups. Fixture decisions are separate from real inference. Recorded Groq runs independently exercised working and broken persistence, and the latest public-site run passed both Wikipedia checks. Type checking, lint, and the production build also passed.

Why Does Open Innovation Matter?

For ProofPack, openness makes the automation inspectable and adaptable.

The source exposes how plans are validated, which actions are permitted, how assertions work, and how evidence becomes a report. Someone can change those rules instead of depending on an opaque demonstration service.

The adapter boundary also separates model choice from browser execution. Groq with GPT-OSS 120B is the configuration I actually verified. OpenRouter and local OpenAI-compatible endpoints are implemented, but real inference through those paths remains unverified.

The current demonstration is therefore not offline. Briefs and bounded page observations are sent to Groq. Screenshots and traces remain local.

I also keep the application’s MIT license separate from model licensing. Open components offer useful control and replacement options; they do not remove the need to validate outputs or check behavior.

The Lazy Payoff

During the build, ProofPack performed the repeated account creation, project creation, logout, fresh-session login, and persistence checks against LaunchDesk. It also performed the public Wikipedia search and collected its evidence.

That replaces a concrete sequence of manual browser interactions and evidence assembly. I did not measure a comparable manual baseline, so I am not claiming a particular number of minutes saved.

The user still defines success, configures allowed targets, reviews the proposed coverage and results, and investigates failures. ProofPack does not establish that an application is bug-free or support every website workflow.

The payoff is having the exercised steps and their evidence ready to inspect, rather than having to repeat the walkthrough and piece the explanation together afterward.

title: # My First Open-Source Contribution 🚀
summary:
I recently took my first step into open-source development by contributing to DevLinks 01.

For my first contribution, I worked on a small issue involving a typo in the main heading. The word “Wecome” needed to be corrected to “Welcome” in src/components/Header.jsx.

Although the change was small, it gave me an opportunity to understand how contributing to an existing codebase works. I worked on a separate branch, made the change, and submitted a pull request rather than directly modifying the main branch.

One thing I learned from this experience is that open-source contributions aren't always about building big features. Even small fixes matter because they improve the quality and usability of a project. I also got more familiar with the Git workflow and the importance of keeping changes focused so they are easier to review.

AI was useful as a learning aid during my development workflow, but I learned that suggestions should never be accepted blindly. It's important to inspect the actual code changes and verify the result instead of assuming that an answer is correct.

My first contribution has encouraged me to explore more repositories, understand issues before jumping into solutions, and become more confident about contributing to projects maintained by other developers.

I'm looking forward to making more contributions, learning from code reviews, and improving with every pull request!

Project: DevLinks 01

My PR: https://github.com/IshaRode/devlinks-01/pull/56

OpenSource #FirstContribution #GitHub #LearningInPublic

title: I built a sloth-brained Downloads folder tidier that runs 100% offline
summary:
This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 3: Slow and Steady

What I Built

My Downloads folder is a landfill: scan0001.pdf, final_v3(2).docx, IMG_4471.png. I never clean it because deciding where each file goes is exactly the kind of tiny chore I avoid.

lazy-downloads-tidier watches the folder, reads each file, and asks a local LLM two questions: which of my categories does this belong in? and what should it be called? Then it moves it to Tidy//YYYY-MM-DD_descriptive-title.ext. I set it up once, and the chore is gone.

Demo

Code

laiba-Ashfaq / lazy-downloads-tidier

🦥 lazy-downloads-tidier

A local LLM that reads your messy Downloads folder, gives each file a meaningful name, and files it into folders. Runs fully offline. Your files never leave your machine.

Downloads/scan0001.pdf   ->  Tidy/Finance/2026-10-19_electricity-bill-september.pdf
Downloads/IMG_4471.png   ->  Tidy/Media/2026-10-18_whiteboard-sprint-plan.png
Downloads/final_v3(2).docx -> Tidy/Work/2026-10-12_q3-marketing-report.docx

Setup (about 3 minutes)

  1. Install Ollama and pull a model 
    ollama pull qwen2.5:7b      # or gemma3:4b / llama3.2:3b for less RAM
  2. Python 3.11+. No pip packages needed. (Optional: pdftotext from poppler for PDF reading.)
  3. Edit config.toml: set your folders, model, and categories.

Use

python tidier.py run             # dry run, prints the plan, moves nothing
python tidier.py run --apply     # do it
python tidier.py watch --apply   # leave it running, tidies new downloads
python tidier.py undo            # reverse the last batch

Safety, because lazy shouldn't mean reckless

  • Dry run by default. You must pass --apply to move anything.
  • Undo log. Every move is recorded in Tidy/.tidier-log.jsonl.
  • Never overwrites. Name…
View on GitHub

How I Built It

  • Model: an open-weight model served by Ollama (default qwen2.5:7b; gemma3:4b or llama3.2:3b for smaller machines).
  • Zero dependencies: one stdlib-only Python file. It calls Ollama's local HTTP API and asks for JSON output at temperature 0.
  • Text extraction: plain text and code directly, .docx by reading the XML inside the zip, PDFs via pdftotext. Images and binaries are classified from filename and extension.
  • Guardrails: the model can only choose from the categories in my config.toml; anything else falls back to Misc. Filenames are slugified, collisions get _v2, and in-progress downloads are skipped.
  • Safety: dry run by default, plus an append-only log that powers undo.

Why Does Open Innovation Matter?

  • Privacy. This tool reads my tax PDFs, contracts, and personal photos. Sending those to someone else's API to get a better filename isn't a trade I'd make. With a local model, the files never leave the disk.
  • Cost. Per-file API pricing is a bad fit for "process my whole backlog of 3,000 files." Locally, the marginal cost is zero, so I can run it on everything, repeatedly, while tuning it.
  • Works offline. No internet means no problem.
  • Swappable and tunable. Changing models is one line in the config. My filing rules are plain-English category descriptions I can rewrite whenever I like, and with open weights I could fine-tune on my own past filing decisions.
  • No rug-pull. The model on my machine won't be deprecated, repriced, or silently changed under my script.

The Lazy Payoff

Prize Categories

_Best Use of Gemma: _the whole tool runs on Gemma (gemma3:1b) locally through Ollama, with no cloud calls.

Best Use of GitHub Copilot / GitHub: the project is automated with GitHub Actions, which runs the tests on every push on Ubuntu and Windows.

_Best Use of ElevenLabs: _the demo narration was generated with ElevenLabs.

title: Eight pre-registered tests on U.S. power plants that slip a month: what held, and what I take back
summary:
EIA's monthly generator inventory, EIA-860M, lists generators planned to start next month. Fewer than four in ten of them are listed as operating in that month now, against almost half in 2016-2019. Over the last few days I ran eight tests on why, and on whether a generator's earlier slips say anything about its next month. Each test's predictions were published before the job that scored them counted anything. 27 of the 33 predictions held.

What still stands. Pooled over 2016-2025, a solar generator planned for next month again right after a one-month slip was listed as operating in that month about 5 percentage points more often than a new solar listing, and a battery about 8 points more often. For solar since 2022, a slip of 2-3 months has been a bad sign: 12.5 points worse than a one-month slip. These three gaps hold when whole plants are resampled 2,000 times, so they are not the work of a few big plants.

What I take back. In my last post I wrote that gas and wind go the other way, and a later test on 2020-2021 seemed to confirm it for wind. With whole plants resampled, the wind and gas gaps are within plant-to-plant noise in every period. The same is true for all technologies together: a one-month slip is not shown to be a good sign on its own. One test that weighted each plant once failed two predictions, and the reason was the method, not the plants: that weighting lifts every repeat-listing group by construction.

Two things to keep in mind:

  • These are generator-months, and "on time" means the next monthly file lists the generator as operating. Resampling plants handles dependence inside a plant, not between plants of one developer or region. These are rates for groups, not forecasts for one generator.
  • The next test is the first on months that do not exist yet: October to December 2026, fixed before EIA publishes its October file on 24 November.

The summary note with every prediction and outcome, the code, the raw output and the tests that check every number are here: https://github.com/munimtechnologies/eia860m-slip

I am MV2 of Munim, Inc. The code, data compilation and this post were made with AI agents working in my name.
